Empirical Research Plan: “M&A and Mark-Up Pricing in the Finance Sector, 1980-1995”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DiD) / Event-Study with Propensity-Score-Re-Weighting.

Why this strategy is appropriate

•  Treatment (an M&A announcement) is sharply timed and plausibly exogenous to very near-term pricing, giving an event-style break.  
•  We observe the same firms for many quarters pre- and post-event → panel DiD makes use of rich within-firm variation and eliminates all time-invariant firm characteristics.  
•  Other finance-sector firms that do not undertake/receive an acquisition in the sample window provide a contemporaneous counterfactual, satisfying the “common shocks” demand of DiD.  
•  Because acquisitions occur in different quarters (staggered adoption), we implement the Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) or Sun-Abraham (2021) estimator to avoid the known biases of two-way-fixed-effects under treatment heterogeneity.  
•  Pre-merger observables (size, profitability, loan mix, geographic footprint, stock β) predict treatment propensity; we will balance on these via inverse-probability weights so that treated and control firms look similar on pre-trends and covariates.  

Alternative considerations (IV using regulatory shocks, regression discontinuity in merger review, etc.) are infeasible with the information supplied; DiD is the tightest credible approach given the data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TREATED_it = 1 for firm i in quarters τ ≥ 0, where τ = 0 is the first quarter whose entire 90-day span occurs after the public M&A announcement date (announcement, not completion, is the information shock). TREATED_it = 0 otherwise.

Control group  
All finance-sector firms in the dataset that (a) never announce an M&A deal during the sample window (“pure controls”) or (b) announce only after the current event’s observation window and are still untreated at time t (“not-yet-treated” controls). For staggered estimators, these groups are combined in the appropriate comparison set per period.

Timing / variation  
Key variation is the within-firm change in markup from the pre-treatment window (t = -8 to ‑1 quarters) to post-treatment window (t = 0 to +8). With staggered DiD, every announcement quarter generates its own comparison with controls in the same calendar quarter, eliminating aggregate confounds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent the M&A, treated firms’ markups would have followed the same mean trajectory as control firms.  
Plausibility: Finance-sector markups are driven by macro factors (rates, regulation) common to all firms; balancing on pre-treatment growth and covariates further supports the assumption.

A2. No differential anticipation: Firms do not change markups in the few quarters immediately before announcement due to leaked information.  
Plausibility: Public disclosure rules and penalties reduce early price changes; we will nevertheless drop τ = -1 and test for pre-trends.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers): One firm’s merger does not materially alter competitors’ markups within the short-run estimation window.  
Plausibility: In the finance sector, competitive effects could create spillovers; we will check robustness using geographic market definitions and drop closest rivals.

A4. Consistent treatment timing: Announcement dates are precisely measured (SEC filings, Dow Jones tapes).  
Plausibility: Regulatory filings provide reliable dates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Selection on unobserved trends (violates A1)  
   •  Pre-merger growth could predict both treatment and later markups.  
   •  Remedy: Show graphical and statistical pre-trend tests; use firm-specific time trends; employ propensity-score weighting and covariate-adjusted DiD.

2. Anticipatory pricing changes (violates A2)  
   •  Remedy: Include leads of treatment in an event-study; if coefficients at τ = -4…-2 are small and insignificant, retain design; otherwise shift τ = 0 backward or censor early quarters.

3. Spillovers to competitors (violates A3)  
   •  Remedy: Construct “clean” control group of firms in different 3-digit SIC markets and in non-overlapping states; alternatively, instrument post-treatment markups of controls with lagged values to purge contemporaneous influence; run robustness where controls within the same market are dropped.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0) Libraries
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast FE regressions
library(did)           # Callaway & Sant'Anna
library(MatchIt)       # Propensity matching
library(ggplot2)

# 1) Data Loading
dt <- fread("finance_mna_quarterly.csv")   # assume wide panel

# 2) Basic Variable Construction
dt[, announce_qtr := as.Date(announce_date) %/% months(3) * 3]  # floor to quarter
dt[, qtr := as.Date(date) %/% months(3) * 3]

# Event time (quarters relative to announcement)
dt[, rel_qtr := as.integer((qtr - announce_qtr)/months(3))]
dt[, treated := !is.na(announce_date)]
dt[, post := as.integer(rel_qtr >= 0 & treated==TRUE)]

# Keep balanced panel around event ±8 qtrs
dt_event <- dt[rel_qtr >= -8 & rel_qtr <= 8]

# 3) Propensity Score (pre-treatment covariates averaged over −8…−1)
pre_cov <- dt_event[rel_qtr < 0,
        .(size = mean(log(assets)),
          roa  = mean(roa),
          leverage = mean(leverage),
          pre_markup_trend = coef(lm(markup ~ qtr))[2]),
        by = firm_id]

ps_model <- glm(treated ~ size + roa + leverage + pre_markup_trend,
                data = pre_cov, family = binomial)
pre_cov[, ps := predict(ps_model, type="response")]

# Merge weights back
dt_event <- merge(dt_event, pre_cov[, .(firm_id, ps)], by="firm_id", all.x=TRUE)
dt_event[, ipw := treated/ps + (1-treated)/(1-ps)] # inverse prob. weights

# 4) Main DiD (Sun & Abraham) using fixest with weights
event_spec <- feols(markup ~ sunab(announce_qtr, qtr) | firm_id + qtr,
                    data = dt_event,
                    weights = ~ipw, cluster = "firm_id")

etable(event_spec, se = "cluster")

# 5) Alternative: Callaway-Sant'Anna
cs <- att_gt(yname="markup",
             tname="announce_qtr",
             idname="firm_id",
             gname="first_treat_qtr",  # create this first
             xformla=~ size + roa + leverage,
             data=dt_event,
             est_method="dr",
             control_group="notyettreated")
agg_effects <- aggte(cs, type="dynamic")
summary(agg_effects)
ggdid(agg_effects)

# 6) Robustness Check: Drop firms in same SIC3 market
sic3_overlap <- merge(dt_event[treated==TRUE,.(sic3_unique=unique(sic3))], dt_event, by.x="sic3_unique", by.y="sic3")
dt_rb <- dt_event[!firm_id %in% sic3_overlap[treated==FALSE]$firm_id]
rb_spec <- feols(markup ~ sunab(announce_qtr, qtr) | firm_id + qtr,
                 data = dt_rb, cluster="firm_id")
etable(rb_spec)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that horizontal consolidation increases market power and therefore markups.  For the finance sector in the 1980-1995 deregulation era, I expect an average post-merger markup increase of ≈ 2–4 percentage points (≈ 5–10 % relative to an average 40 % gross margin) within two years after announcement.  Heterogeneity: bigger effects for in-market mergers, negligible or zero for diversifying mergers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = weak)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Balance / Overlap between treated and control units …… 0.8  
2. Parallel pre-trends (graphical & statistical) …………… 0.7  
3. No anticipation / information leakage …………………… 0.6  
4. No spillovers / interference …………………………………… 0.5  
5. Correct DiD estimator for staggered treatment ………… 0.9  

Overall, the design is strong but rests primarily on the plausibility of parallel trends and limited spillovers, which must be extensively tested and defended.
